subject: chemistry_2
question_text: Give two examples for gaseous first order reactions.

verification.note: Unit 4 (Chemical Kinetics) is sourced from the chemistry half of "FAST TRACK IPE for Sr. Students", book pp.73-76, which prints the question and a model answer. The 1+1 mark split is a CLAIM, not the board's, until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced, not invented. Neither the two-book union check nor a board back-test was possible for Chemistry-II: the TSBIE Basic Learning Material on hand is physics-only and first-year, and no second-year chemistry paper is in the corpus. Both printed examples are CORRECT and are kept: hydrogenation of ethene, rate = k[C₂H₄], and decomposition of N₂O₅, rate = k[N₂O₅]. BOOK INCONSISTENCY: the book writes the N₂O₅ decomposition here as "N₂O₅(g) → 2NO₂(g) + ½O₂(g)" but on the previous page (VSAQ 3) as "N₂O₅ → N₂O₄ + ½O₂". Both are balanced, but the two forms are never reconciled. The NCERT integer form 2N₂O₅ → 4NO₂ + O₂ is used on this card and on VSAQ 3, so the unit reads consistently. NOTE ON THE FIRST EXAMPLE: the hydrogenation of ethene is measured as first order in ethene, rate = k[C₂H₄], which is the form both the book and NCERT print. An earlier version of this card explained that law by saying hydrogen is taken in excess. Neither source states that condition, and it is the condition this unit uses to define a PSEUDO first order reaction (VSAQ 9), so as written it made this reaction an example of the wrong thing. The card now states the measured law and stops.

steps.label: What first order means
lines: In a first order reaction the rate is
directly proportional to the first power of
The unit of k is s⁻¹.
steps.why: First order is the most common kinetic behaviour for a gas that falls apart on its own, because one molecule breaking up is one event and its chance per second does not depend on how many other molecules are nearby.
common_mistakes: Writing rate = k[A]² and still calling it first order. The power on the concentration must be 1.
Giving the unit of k as mol L⁻¹ s⁻¹. For first order the concentration unit cancels and only s⁻¹ is left.
steps.memory_tip: First order: double the concentration and the rate exactly doubles.
steps.margin_note: Write rate = k[A] before the examples. It is what makes each example an illustration.

steps.why: The second example is the stronger one, because the balanced equation has a 2 in front of N₂O₅ and the measured order is still 1. It answers the question and shows at the same time that the order is not read off the equation.
common_mistakes: Writing the rate law for the hydrogenation as k[C₂H₄][H₂]. The order is not read off the equation; the measured law is first order in ethene.
Giving a reaction in solution. The question asks for gaseous reactions, so every species must be marked (g).
steps.memory_tip: Ethene plus hydrogen, and N₂O₅ decomposing. Both gases, both first order.
steps.margin_note: Write the rate law under each equation and mark the states (g). The word gaseous is part of the question.
